claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its FCC quaternary and ternary subsets arise from composition-induced variations in stacking-fault energy rather than constituent count alone.
The presence of Mn lowers the stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy relative to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Lower stacking-fault energy may promote a strain-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Changes in twinning activity alter strain-hardening behavior.
The controlled comparison is restricted to single-phase FCC quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
The compared alloys will have comparable grain size and texture.
In situ TEM, slip-trace analysis, and stacking-fault-energy determination can distinguish the active deformation modes in the controlled tests.
The comparison will use room-temperature tension and compression at controlled strain rates.
Identical thermomechanical processing histories will be used across the alloy compositions.
Local stacking-fault energy modulates active slip systems and twin-nucleation dynamics.
The quinary alloy will begin deformation twinning at a lower strain than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy may exhibit an FCC-to-HCP transformation earlier or more readily than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Quantitative measurements will show a lower stacking-fault energy for the quinary alloy than for the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The proposed mechanism applies only to comparably processed, single-phase FCC alloys deformed at room temperature.
Local chemical ordering may also contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
Identical stacking-fault energies, similar twinning-onset strains, and identical dominant deformation mechanisms across all compared alloys would falsify the proposed SFE-mediated explanation.
